content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Write electronic configurations for the first 20 elements
Relate electronic configuration to position in the periodic table
Use position to predict electronic configuration and vice versa
Explain why group number relates to outer electrons
of an element determines its position in the periodic table and its chemical properties. Understanding this relationship allows you to predict properties from position and vice versa.
Once a shell is full, the next electron goes to the next shell
The Link to the Periodic Table
Group number = Number of electrons in outer shell
Period number = Number of electron shells
Elements in the same group have similar properties because:
Same way of achieving stable configuration
Similar reactions (lose, gain, or share same number of electrons)
All lose 1 electron to form +1 ions
All gain 1 electron to form -1 ions
[DIAGRAM: Electron shell diagrams for Na (2,8,1), Cl (2,8,7), and Ar (2,8,8) showing electrons in shells]
Place electrons in pairs where possible
1st shell: max 2; 2nd shell: max 8; 3rd shell: max 8
Write the electronic configuration for sulfur (atomic number 16) and state its group and period.
An element has electronic configuration 2,8,8,1. Identify the element and predict its properties.
Forms K⁺ ions by losing 1 electron
Explain why sodium and potassium have similar chemical properties.
Both have the same number of outer electrons
Both lose 1 electron easily to achieve a stable configuration
Chemical properties depend on outer electrons
Predict the electronic configuration of an element in Group 7, Period 4.
Putting more than 8 electrons in the 2nd or 3rd shell (at this level)
For elements 1-20, shells hold 2, 8, 8, then continue
Confusing group number with total electrons
Thinking Group 0 elements have 0 outer electrons
Group 0 have FULL outer shells (8 electrons, or 2 for He)
